activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: To avoid feedback, microphones should not be pointed at the loudspeakers or held in front of them.
story:
Jordan had one night before his first school concert, and his grandfather's old microphone was supposed to be retired years ago, but tonight it sat on the kitchen table next to the speaker Dad had set up for practice. The speaker was decorated with paper tropical flowers left over from Mom's birthday party, which made the whole thing look strangely festive. Jordan had begged to practice exactly the way it would feel on stage, standing up, holding the microphone, singing his six lines of the solo over the backing track. Keegan was coming over at seven, and after that there would be no more time.

The first run-through went fine. On the second, Jordan stepped forward to hit the loud note, and a scream tore out of the speaker, a high howl that made him drop his arm and made Dad come running from the garage. "What did you touch?" Dad asked, checking the wires. Jordan hadn't touched anything. He stood where he had been, in front of the speaker, microphone still raised toward it, and nothing happened. The howl had come and gone like something alive.

He decided to test it. He walked the same path again, slow, watching the speaker out of the corner of his eye. Nothing. Then he turned to face the crowd of kitchen chairs he had arranged as an audience, and the microphone swung around with him and pointed straight at the speaker, and the howl rose again until he angled it away. "It's when it points at the speaker," he told Keegan when he arrived. "Or when you stand right in front of it." He made Keegan sit in a chair and watch, and they ran it five times, and every single time the rule held. He practiced keeping the microphone aimed at the chairs, never back at the tropical flowers, until his hand did it without thinking. That had been a close call with the concert only hours away, and he sat in the dark living room afterward wondering whether he should have practiced with the speaker days ago instead of putting it off for card trades. His trade with Keegan had ended in a settlement of three comics, and now the comics seemed like a bad bargain.

At the concert the next evening, the soloist before him, a girl from another class, moved downstage for her big finish, and the microphone crept up until it aimed at the tall speaker at the edge of the stage. Jordan heard the howl start to build, thin and rising. He leaned forward from the second row of the choir and caught her eye, and he pointed, quick and small, at the speaker. She turned the microphone toward the audience instead, and the howl faded, and her voice rang out clean over the last chord. Ms. García, directing from the pit, looked over her glasses at Jordan. "You knew that was coming," she said. He smiled and gripped his own microphone, aimed nowhere near a speaker.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: A frost, hailstorm or drought that ruins part of a strawberry crop reduces the supply, which pushes the price of the remaining berries up.
story:
Natalie squeezed the last of the lemons into the pitcher and looked down the sidewalk. Her lemonade stand had earned four dollars all morning, and the strawberries stacked in a bowl beside the cups had earned nothing at all, because she had priced them at two dollars each and nobody would pay it.

"Two dollars for one strawberry?" said Bodhi, who lived three houses down and stopped by every Saturday. "The berry stand by the farm market sells a whole basket for less than that."

"They did last summer," Natalie said. "I checked the board this morning. The price went way up this week." She held up her phone so he could see the photo she had taken of the hand-lettered sign.

Kylian pedaled up the street, dropped his bike in the grass, and read the sign taped to Natalie's table. "Strawberries, two dollars. Why so expensive?"

"There was a frost," said a parent weeding next door, without looking up. "Tuesday night. Took out a good part of the crop."

Kylian frowned at the bowl. "So the berries that didn't freeze get more expensive? That doesn't seem fair to the berries."

Natalie turned the idea over while she poured him a lemonade. Fewer strawberries existed now, she thought, but the same number of people wanted them, so the ones left cost more. Last winter she had saved her allowance for weeks to buy strawberries for her grandmother's birthday cake, and she remembered standing in the store feeling cheated by the price, until her mother said it was just the season. She had accepted that then. Now she wondered whether she was doing the same thing to her neighbors that had once irritated her.

She taped a new sign over the old one. "Strawberries, fifty cents, because the frost was not their fault." Bodhi bought three. Kylian bought two and ate one immediately.

Mr. González, who taught at the school and lived on the corner, walked by with his dog and paused at the table. "Lowered your price? I thought everything costs more after a frost."

"Strawberries do," Natalie said. "At the farm stand. Mine don't, because mine are just the regular ones from the store. But next week, when the farms pick what's left, I'm going to track the price every day and see when it falls again." She was already picturing the notebook page, columns waiting for numbers.

Mr. González bought a lemonade and a strawberry and said he wanted to see her data. Kylian leaned over the bowl and asked if she thought the price would ever drop all the way back down, or if the farms would just get used to charging more.

"I don't know yet," Natalie said, and flipped her notebook open to a clean page.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In parts of North America, blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease, so campers there check their skin and hair for ticks after hiking through woods or tall grass.
story:
Livia laid everything out on her bed like a general planning a battle: two swimsuits, a rain jacket, a flashlight, and the long plastic comb with the teeth close together. The dryer downstairs radiated warm air up through the floorboards, and she could hear her dad arguing with the tent bag, which always won.

She picked up the comb and thought about Monica. Last August, Monica had come back from Camp Wrenfield with a whole report delivered on Livia's front steps. "Every night after hiking, we line up and the counsellor checks behind our ears and in our hair," Monica had said, picking at her mosquito bites. "Blacklegged ticks, they also call them deer ticks, can spread Lyme disease in some parts of North America, so we have to check." Livia had rolled her eyes at the time. Checking your own head for a bug the size of a poppy seed seemed like busywork, like something camps invented to fill ten minutes before lights out.

Now she wasn't so sure. She turned the comb over in her hands and ran through the logic like a math problem. A tick could crawl onto you in the woods or in tall grass, and it hid. You wouldn't feel it. That meant the only way to know was to look, every night, because a missed tick wasn't like a missed homework assignment. Monica had missed one check, one single night, because she was tired, and she'd found the tick two days later on the back of her knee. She'd had to go to the doctor. She still didn't know, she told Livia, whether one skipped night was what did it, or whether the tick had come off during some other check. It bothered her, that not knowing.

Livia decided to test the comb. She went out to the back corner of the yard, where the grass grew tall and wild because the mower couldn't reach past the fence, and she waded through it twice, dragging her hand along the seed heads. Then, back inside, she stood at the bathroom mirror and worked the comb through her hair in slow rows, section by section, exactly like Monica had described. Nothing. She checked twice, because a first check with nothing found wasn't proof of anything except that she hadn't found anything.

On the way back to her room she stopped to pump her bike tire, but the valve was bent and the pump wouldn't seal, so the bike stayed in the garage, sulking. She found her old camp whistle from two summers ago, the orange plastic one, and held it up. It was basically obsolete now, since Camp Wrenfield issued whistles to everyone, but she packed it anyway, tucked into the side pocket next to the comb.

Her dad appeared in the doorway with the defeated tent bag under one arm. "Ready, scout?"

"Almost." She held up the comb. "Do you want to practice checking my hair now, so you don't get rusty while I'm gone?"

He laughed and set the bag down. "Come here, then. Sit by the window where the light's better."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: A standard AA battery provides about 1.5 volts.
story:
Taylor knelt on the grass beside a shoebox full of wires, clips, a little bulb, a switch, and a single AA battery. "Today I become competent," she announced to the compost bin, which was busy helping old leaves decompose and did not answer.

Laurel dropped down beside her, sucking a juice box. "What's all this?"

"Circuit," Taylor said. "Battery, switch, bulb. If I build it right, the bulb lights when I flip the switch." She clipped the wires on, taped everything to a board, and pressed the switch. Nothing. The bulb sat there like a tiny glass grump.

"You wired it backwards," said Laurel.

"You can't wire electricity backwards, it's not a bicycle." Taylor frowned at the bulb. The wires all looked connected. Then she remembered the label on the battery's side. She flipped it over and squinted. "Laurel. It says one point five volts."

"Is that a lot?"

Taylor held up the bulb and read its box, which had tumbled out from under a trowel. "Three volts. So one battery is like half a sandwich." She chewed her lip, thinking. Two halves make a whole. She ran inside, dug through the kitchen drawer where dead batteries went to retire, and came back holding another AA, warm from her pocket like a hamster.

"Each one gives one point five volts," she said, snapping the two batteries end to end, "so together they make three. Exactly what the bulb wants." She rebuilt the circuit, clipped the last wire, and rested her thumb on the switch. "Laurel, do the honors of silence."

Laurel saluted with her juice box.

Taylor flipped the switch. The bulb glowed, small and stubborn and golden, like a firefly that had decided to stay for dinner.

Laurel leaned in until her nose almost touched the glass. "It's so little. And smug."

"It should be smug," Taylor said. "It took us two batteries and one backyard."

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: Putting quotation marks around a phrase asks Google to find pages containing those exact words in that exact order.
story:
Lea's grandmother used to hum a song about a river running backward, and now that Grandma had moved far away, Lea wanted to find that song more than anything. She typed river running backward song into the search bar and got a flood of results: a game about rivers, a music video by someone shouting about trucks, and, at the very top, a bright box promising "River Songs for Less!" with a Buy Now button.

"Hold on," Lea said to herself. She leaned closer to the screen. The top result had a tiny label, easy to miss unless you were looking. She squinted at it. It said ad, in small gray letters, and once she noticed the first one, she saw them everywhere, like spotting the same weed in every garden bed. The ads sat at the top of the page as if they were the best answers, but were they? She wondered whether the real results were the plain ones underneath, the ones nobody had paid to place there.

Khalil had once told her that search results had their own order, a kind of hierarchy, and that the top spots could be bought. That gave her an idea. She scrolled past the ads and found pages about folk songs, but none of them mentioned a river running backward. Her search was too vague. The words could appear in any order, anywhere. What if she could ask for the exact words?

She tried something. Grandma always sang the same odd line: "the water remembers where it came from." Lea typed the whole phrase with quotation marks around it, like a paper doll cut out in one piece, and pressed Enter. The results changed completely. Every single page now contained that exact phrase, in that exact order. She sat back, amazed. The quotation marks had told the search engine to find those precise words together, nothing scrambled or rearranged.

The third result down, no ad label on it, was a folk archive listing a lullaby from the 1960s titled "The Water Remembers." Lea clicked it, and a scratchy recording began to play. It was the song. She hummed along, then texted Khalil: guess what quotation marks do. Three guesses.

Khalil wrote back, "I give up. Tell me at school."

"Tomorrow," she typed, and turned up the volume so the whole kitchen could hear Grandma's river running backward.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin Chinese puts a measure word between a number and a noun: "one cat" is "yì zhī māo," where "zhī" is the measure word used for many animals.
story:
Xavier spread his flashcards across the kitchen table even though the room was so humid the cards stuck slightly to the wood. On the laptop screen, his grandmother in Guangzhou sipped her tea and waited, because tonight he had promised to describe the whole family in Mandarin, in full sentences, before Friday's culture share at school. Karissa had already texted him three times. She wanted their class presentation to include a video of a real conversation, not just posters, and she had volunteered Xavier as the star whether he liked it or not.

He began with the easy one. "Wǒ yǒu yì māo," he said, meaning he had one cat, and he pointed the camera at Olive, who was asleep on the windowsill.

His grandmother held up one finger and smiled. "Yì zhī māo," she said gently. "You need zhī."

Xavier wrote it down fast. So a number and an animal needed something in the middle, a little word, zhī, that didn't mean anything by itself but held the sentence together. He had never noticed it before because his ear kept skipping over small sounds. He decided to test it right away, because Karissa would ask questions on Friday and he did not want to guess. "Wǒ yǒu liǎng zhī māo?" he asked, holding up two fingers.

His grandmother laughed and shook her head. "Only one Olive," she said, "but yes, the zhī is correct. Liǎng zhī māo. Very good."

He tried a dog next. "Sān zhī gǒu." She nodded, so the little word worked for dogs too, and probably for many animals, which felt like finding a hidden lever inside the language. He was so excited he stood up, and Olive bolted off the windowsill as if the applause were already starting.

They recorded the video twice, and the second take was perfect, even with Olive's tail drifting across the corner of the frame. Xavier made one small amendment to his script on paper, printing ZHĪ in capital letters with a star beside it. Karissa texted a row of exclamation marks when he sent the file. At the end, his grandmother lifted her jade bracelet toward the camera. "This bracelet," she said, "it symbolize family, round, no beginning, no end." Xavier repeated the word in Mandarin, then in English, then pointed at Olive and said, clear as a bell, "Yì zhī māo."

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: Most tuners use A = 440 hertz as the reference note, meaning the A above middle C vibrates 440 times a second, though some orchestras tune slightly higher.
story:
Thomas sat on the living room rug with his grandfather's guitar, which had been dormant in the closet for years, its strings dull and floppy. He wanted to play one real song for his mum by Sunday, and he could not do that with a guitar that sounded like a wet sock.

He had a tuner app on his mum's old phone, and when he plucked the top string, the screen flashed a number: 440. He plucked again and the number jumped to 391. He had no idea what the numbers meant, so he took the phone next door to Mr. Zhao, who repaired instruments in his garage.

"Mr. Zhao, what's 440?"

Mr. Zhao did not launch into a lecture. He only said, "Hertz. Look it up while you work," and handed Thomas a small electronic tuner that hummed one steady note. Thomas held the humming tuner to his ear, then plucked the guitar string and listened. The two notes beat against each other, a wobbling sound like a bird flapping. When he tightened the tuning peg, the wobble slowed. When the two notes finally matched, the wobble vanished and the string rang clear alongside the tuner. So that was it: he could hear when a note was wrong, and he could hear the moment it became right, without looking at any screen.

Back at home he looked up the number for himself. Most tuners, the page said, use A = 440 hertz as the reference note, meaning the A above middle C vibrates 440 times a second, though some orchestras tune slightly higher. Four hundred and forty vibrations every single second, invisible but real, hiding inside a sound.

Then came the twist. When he tuned the fattest string, it refused to match no matter how carefully he turned the peg, and the wobbling beat stayed stubborn. He reasoned it out: the small string had worked because it matched the tuner's A. This fat string had to match a different note, so the hidden pattern must repeat itself lower down. He pressed the fifth fret, plucked, and matched that note to the tuner's hum instead. The wobble vanished.

He could not convey how the guitar suddenly felt alive under his hands, so he carried it to the kitchen and played his one song, all six strings ringing together. His mum put down the dish towel.

"Play that part again," she said.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes.
story:
At 8:14 on Tuesday night, Easton's phone emitted a soft buzz against his desk. The group chat, dormant since Friday, had sprung to life. Twenty-three messages scrolled past, all because of one line Easton had typed after school: "Leopold's corn snake got loose in the cafeteria and the lunch ladies are evacuating." He had leaned back in his chair, pleased with himself, imagining Salim laughing. But the messages weren't laughter. Someone had sent a screenshot to the principal. Someone's mother had already called the school. Someone had written, "I'm not eating in that cafeteria ever again."

Easton typed "it was a joke" and stared at the words. On the screen they looked exactly as serious as everything else. There was no way to show a grin through text, no raised eyebrow, no smirk. He deleted the message, retyped it, deleted it again. His thumb hovered. Meanwhile the chat filled with plans: a snake lockdown, a search of the vents, a petition to move lunch to the gym. At the bottom, Salim kept pushing for one thing only. "If the cafeteria is closed," Salim wrote, "they'll have to cancel the science quiz. We should all email the office." Easton reread that three times and felt something cold settle in his stomach.

The next morning, Mr. Popal, who taught music and directed the orchestra, found Easton standing frozen outside the office door. "You look like a conductor who's lost his score," Mr. Popal said. "Whatever it is, breathe first." Easton didn't breathe first. He blurted out the whole thing, the joke, the panic, the screenshot he'd just learned about. What he didn't say was the question burning in his head: who had sent it to the principal, and why?

In the library at lunch, Easton hunted through the internet for a solution and found something better than a solution. He read the page twice, then a third time, mouthing the words. Then he pulled Salim down into the seat beside him. "Listen to this. Scott Fahlman proposed the emoticon on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes." He turned the screen so Salim could see the little sideways smile. "That's the whole reason it exists. People couldn't tell jokes from serious stuff, forty years before I was born."

Salim went pale in a way Easton had never seen. "Okay, fine, I sent the screenshot," Salim said. "I wanted the quiz cancelled. I didn't think they'd call a lockdown." Easton typed a new message to the chat, slow and careful, checking each word: "Yesterday's snake post was a joke. The snake is fine. The snake was always fine. :-)" He hit send, and one by one the replies started coming in.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
story:
When the nurse sawed off Eva's cast, Eva stared at her right arm and laughed out loud. It looked like a noodle next to her left one. "Why is it so skinny?" she asked, and the nurse only smiled and said she'd figure it out.

Back in Ms. Taylor's classroom, Eva couldn't stop comparing. She held both arms out on her desk, one beside the other, and noticed that the right one was paler, too, with flaky skin. Six weeks ago, before the fall off the swing at Logan's birthday party, both arms had matched exactly. She remembered lying in the grass, Gregory shouting "Don't move it, don't move it!" while Logan ran for his mom. Six weeks in a cast, six weeks of doing nothing. She flexed her left arm, and the muscle bunched up like a small hill. She flexed the right one, and almost nothing happened. Was that the factor she was missing, the stillness itself? She tried a test. She wrote her name ten times with her left hand, then squeezed a stress ball Ms. Taylor kept on her desk, twenty careful squeezes. Her arm trembled on the last five. Weak, definitely weak.

"Logan," she whispered across the aisle, "your arm muscles get smaller when they're stuck in a cast and can't move. That's why it looks thinner after. The muscles kind of shrink."

Logan looked at his own arm, which had never been in a cast, and looked a little disappointed. "So if I never moved my legs, would they turn into noodles too?"

"Theoretically," Eva said, pleased with the word.

Ms. Taylor, who had overheard while handing out papers, raised an eyebrow. "Eva, is the stress ball more interesting than fractions?"

"It's for science," Eva said, and squeezed it once more, watching the noodle arm shake.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Havdalah ceremony uses a cup of wine or grape juice, fragrant spices to smell, and a braided candle with several wicks.
story:
The sky outside Grandma's window was almost dark, which meant the clock was running out on Shabbat, and Kate's little brother was about to ruin everything. He had been promised he could hold the braided candle for the first time tonight, and now he was hiding behind the couch because he was afraid the several wicks would drip on his fingers. Kate needed him calm in the next ten minutes or Grandma would say he was too young after all, and he would cry, and the whole evening would be spoiled.

"It's going to hinder everybody if you stay back there," Kate said, crouching down beside the couch. "Grandma can't start without the candle holder. That's you."

"Is it hot?"

Kate considered lying, but a lie had to be plausible, and her brother could smell a lie the way Grandma could smell burnt toast. "A little warm," she said. "The trick is where you hold it. Watch." She pulled the candle box from the sideboard and showed him the braid, the wax strands twisted together like bread. She put her hand well below the several wicks. "You hold it here, by the braid, and the drips fall away from you." She watched his face work through the idea, the way he always did, testing whether a thing made sense before he trusted it.

At the table, Grandma poured grape juice into the special cup until it reached the very top, almost brimming. She passed around the little spice box, its clove smell sharp and sweet, and everyone took a turn breathing it in. Kate sniffed, watching the juice, and noticed something: Grandma had filled that cup to overflowing at the end of every Shabbat she could remember, not just tonight, not just when there were guests. There was a pattern there, some reason she did it on purpose, though Kate couldn't see what the reason was. She decided to test it. "Grandma," she said, "next week could I pour the cup? I'll fill it right to the top."

Grandma's eyes crinkled. "We'll see, the protagonist of the evening," she said, because Kate had grumbled last week that all she ever got to do was watch.

Then it was time. Kate's brother stepped forward with the candle, and Abdulrahman, who had come over after dinner because he wanted to see how Shabbat ended, lit the wicks with a match. The flames caught one by one, and the room glowed. Kate's brother held the braid steady, lower lip between his teeth, not a single flinch.

"You did it," Kate whispered.

He lifted the candle a little higher, just to prove it.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
Andrew had one job at the cultural festival: guard the donation jar at the Japanese house exhibit while his class collected revenue for the spring trip. Mr. Bekele had been clear about that. He had been less clear about what to do if a visitor actually entered the exhibit, which was a problem, because a visitor was entering it right now, in muddy sneakers.

"Sir, you can't walk in there like that," Andrew called, but the man was already halfway across the tatami mats, leaving damp prints behind him like a trail of evidence. Andrew looked at the entrance. There was a row of shoes by the door, arranged neatly, toes facing out, and beside them a pair of slippers that were clearly waiting for someone. Waiting for him, probably. He tested the idea: if slippers sat at the entrance and shoes sat in a row, then shoes came off here, before the inside, and slippers were what you put on instead. It was a rule you couldn't see written anywhere, but the shoes proved it the way footprints prove a trespasser.

The man was heading toward a low table where Zia's grandmother had set out tea and origami cranes. Andrew stepped out of his own sneakers, slid his feet into the slippers, and hurried after him. "Excuse me! Your shoes!"

The man stopped. "There's no sign," he said.

"There doesn't need to be a sign," said Zia, appearing from behind a paper screen. She pointed at the entrance area. "It's called the genkan. Shoes come off there before you step inside. Everybody's shoes."

The man looked at the neat row, then at his own muddy trail, and went back for his shoes with the expression of someone hoping the floor would forgive him. Andrew fetched a cloth and wiped the mats while Zia's grandmother poured the tea, because the festival's tea ceremony demonstration started at three o'clock and it was already ten to.

"You figured out the genkan thing fast," Zia said.

"I followed the slippers," Andrew said. "They told on everybody."

By two fifty-five the mats were clean, the donations were counted twice, and the man was sitting properly at the low table, holding his cup with both hands the way Corinne had shown him. The gradual stream of visitors through the genkan had grown into a line, each pair of shoes set down neatly, each visitor wobbling into a pair of slippers. When the last of the tea was poured, Zia's grandmother looked at the full jar and said, "Good revenue, and clean floors."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
story:
At the after-school science club, Ms. Eze set two baskets on the table and dropped a marble into the left one. "This is an old experiment called the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985," she said. "Sally puts her marble in her basket and leaves. While she's away, Anne moves it to the other basket. When Sally comes back, where will she look?" Walid said the right basket, because that's where the marble was. Stevie said the same thing, faster. Noemie frowned. That was where the marble was, sure, but Sally hadn't seen it move.

"It's a question about what Sally believes, not where the marble is," Noemie said slowly, and Walid groaned like the idea physically offended him. Ms. Eze only shrugged. "You can generate your own evidence," she said. "Tomorrow the kindergartners visit for the club fair. Bring the puppets."

That night Noemie thought about a time last summer when she had blamed Stevie for eating her birthday chocolate, certain of it, and been wrong. She had believed something that wasn't true, and she'd been ten. Could a four-year-old even imagine somebody else believing something false? She kept turning the question over while she packed the baskets and the elastic band she used to strap the puppets to her backpack.

At the fair, Noemie ran the test on a stream of small children. The four-year-olds, mostly, said Sally would search the basket where she'd left her marble. A three-year-old said the right basket every single time, grinning, as if Sally must know what he knew. Stevie watched, arms crossed, then uncrossed them. "So they're not wrong exactly," he said. "They just haven't hit that yet." Walid crouched by the last child, a small girl twirling the puppet's arm. "Where will Sally look, Lila?" She pointed at the left basket. Noemie wrote it down and slid the marble back into place for the next round.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
The bus hadn't even left the parking lot when Carter shoved his phone at Megan. "Look at this. Two stories about the same poll, and one says support went up ten, the other says it went up twenty-five. Somebody's lying."

Megan took the phone. Behind them, Gianna leaned over the seat, and somebody's duffel bag slid into the aisle with a thump. The first story said support rose from forty percent to fifty percent. The second said the same thing, from forty to fifty, but called it a twenty-five percent increase. "They both say forty to fifty," Megan said slowly. "Same numbers. Same poll."

"So ten and twenty-five can't both be right," Carter said. The bus jerked forward, and the driver told them to sit down, they weren't bears coming out of hibernation, they could settle like human beings.

"Wait." Megan grabbed her notebook and drew it out. Ten of what, though? Going from forty percent to fifty percent was a rise of ten percentage points, that was one way to say it. But she remembered the basketball roster taped up in the gym, where the coach ranked players by shooting, and how a jump from making four out of ten shots to five out of ten was counted. Five was a quarter more than four. Twenty-five percent more. She wrote both phrases side by side and stared at them until her ears felt hot. "Carter. Ten percentage points and twenty-five percent. It's the same change, told two ways. Both stories are true."

Gianna snatched the notebook. "Then the websites knew exactly what they were doing," she said. "Big number sounds like big news."

"Exactly!" Megan said. "Nobody lied, they just picked the louder version."

Carter sat back, looking like a plumber who'd finally found the leak. "That's sneaky," he said, and he was already typing a comment, and his first line was almost eloquent: "Same poll, same rise, two different megaphones."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin found deep-sea vent communities whose food chains start with bacteria using chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.
story:
Juliette crouched beside the creek with her notebook open to a blank page. Mr. Yoon had sent them down the nature trail with one job: draw a food chain, start to finish, and be ready to explain what would happen if one link disappeared. She wrote "sun" at the top of the page and underlined it twice.

"That's not a link," Tucker said, looking over her shoulder. "The sun isn't alive."

"It's the start," Juliette said. "Every food chain starts with the sun. Grass grows because of it, rabbits eat the grass, hawks eat the rabbits." She drew an arrow from the sun down to a sketch of grass.

Tucker sat on a flat rock. "Every one? We watched a documentary Friday night. In 1977, scientists went down in a submarine called Alvin and found whole communities of animals down in the deep sea. Tube worms, crabs, all living in total darkness." He pulled a stick from the mud and pointed it at her page. "Their food chain starts with bacteria. The bacteria use chemicals that come out of the vents, not sunlight."

Juliette dismissed that with a wave of her hand, then stopped. "Wait. Total darkness? How deep?" Tucker shrugged. "Deep enough that no sunlight gets there at all." She stared at her underlined "sun." If a chain could start with bacteria and chemicals instead, then the sun was not a rule, it was just the start of most chains, the ones she could see. The whole page suddenly felt like a metaphor that only fit half the world. She flipped to a new page. "Okay, but I can't test the deep sea from a creek."

"You could test the part about links disappearing," Noor said, kneeling in the leaves between them. "Mr. Yoon said to explain that part." Juliette looked at the creek, then at the grass, then up at the treeline where a hawk circled. She drew her chain again, sun to grass to rabbit to hawk, and then erased the rabbit. "If the rabbits go," she said, "the hawks lose their food." Noor traced the chain with one finger. "And if the grass goes, everything above it goes too. The top can't hold up without the bottom. It's not elastic, it can't stretch to fill the gap."

Juliette added a second chain on the same page, vent to bacteria to crab, and drew a circle around the bottom of each one. "Bottom link disappears, whole thing falls," she said. "Doesn't matter if the bottom is grass or bacteria." She capped her pen and stood. From the trail above, Mr. Yoon called that it was time to head back, and Juliette started up the path with the notebook held open so the two chains faced out. "Read it and argue with me," she said to Tucker.

"Read it and agree with you," Tucker said, and he took the creek path two steps at a time to catch up.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
The after-school culture club had one week to build a display for the school festival, and Emile's problem was the word at the top of Charlie's banner. It said DIASPORA in big blue letters, and when Emile asked what it meant, Charlie scratched his head. "My grandpa printed it. He said it's our word. I think it's Greek or something?"

Elaina, who was gluing a map of the world onto their poster board, called across the art room. "Nobody at our table knows either. My aunt wrote it on our banner too." Emile looked around and realized that three tables had banners with the same mystery word, and nobody could explain it. Ms. Haddad, who supervised the club, had made one rule clear at the start: the adults were not permitted to do the projects for the students. "You figure it out," she said whenever anyone asked her a question, smiling like she knew the answer and was enjoying the suspense.

Emile had an objective mind, he liked to think, so he set up a test. He walked to each table and asked the same thing: "Where was your family from, originally?" Charlie's grandparents came from Lebanon but Charlie had been born here. Elaina's family traced back to Jamaica, then England, then here. At the third table a girl said India, but her parents had lived in Kenya first. Emile stared at his notebook. Every family was scattered, living far from where their ancestors had started, and every one of them had that same word on their banner.

"Wait," he said slowly. "It's not a country or a food or a flag. It's the pattern itself." He looked up the word in the dictionary on the shelf and read it twice to be sure, then marched to the front of the room. "It means scattering," he announced. "It comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors." Charlie pumped his fist. "That's why Grandpa printed it! We're the scattering!" The girl at the third table added a scattering of small stars across her map, one for each place her family had lived, and by the end of the afternoon every banner had its own trail of stars, alloying paint and glitter and glue into something none of them could have made alone.

activity: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
knowledge_domain: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
fact: Sound moves faster in water than in air mainly because water is much harder to compress, so each molecule pushes on the next almost at once.
story:
Isabella pressed her ear against the giant steel pipe outside the Echo Room and heard her friend Charlie-Rose whisper "pineapple socks" from the far end, loud and clear. That settled it: she wanted the museum's junior guide badge, and for that she had to explain sound to Ms. Grewal by closing time. Sound, the badge sheet said, including one tricky question about water.

"The problem is you can't see it," Isabella said, pacing. "Sound is invisible. How am I supposed to explain something invisible?"

"Sound is vibrations," said Charlie-Rose, who was mainly here for the gift shop's extinct shark tooth, which she had been saving allowance money for since March. "Mr. Tube-Wisperer here proves it. Feel the pipe while I talk." Isabella laid her palm on the steel and felt the words buzz against her skin like tiny knocking. "Okay, revise my plan," she said, pulling out her notebook. "Vibrations. Step one done."

Step two was the water question, and that was where Lorie found them, elbow-deep in the museum's wave tank, which said DO NOT TOUCH in very polite letters. "I'm not touching, I'm experimenting," Lorie said, though she had also come for the shark tooth and wanted first pick. "Pool day last week, remember? Somebody tapped the wall underwater and we all heard it like a drum. My little brother said it was magic. I want to tell him it isn't."

Isabella stared at the tank. Air was squishy, she thought. You could squeeze a balloon of it. Water, you couldn't squeeze at all, and squeezing was how the vibrations got passed along, molecule to molecule, like a row of people shoving each other. In squishy air, each shove softened first. In water, each molecule pushed the next one almost at once, so the tap shot to your ears before it could get tired. "That's it," she said. "Water's just stubborn. It won't squish, so the push travels fast."

"Prove it," said Lorie. So Isabella borrowed two metal spoons from the snack bar, handed one to Charlie-Rose, and held her breath. Charlie-Rose tapped her spoon above the water, and Isabella heard a small clink. Then Charlie-Rose dunked it and tapped underwater, and Isabella, ears just below the surface, nearly jumped. The clang hit her like a bell inside her skull.

"Ms. Grewal!" Isabella yelled, dripping. Ms. Grewal listened to the whole explanation, tap-tapped the tank herself, and pinned the badge on. Charlie-Rose got her shark tooth. Lorie, sulking by the empty display, got a fossilized clam instead. "Fine," Lorie said, holding it up. "Clams used to hear great underwater too, probably."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: A conductor shows the first beat of each bar, called the downbeat, with a downward movement of the hand or baton.
story:
Willow stood in the back row of the choir loft at St. Brigid's, holding her folder of hymns and listening to the sopranos sail above her. Ms. Tehrani had put her on the second part, the lower harmony, and had said it would take some getting used to. Willow had thought singing was just singing, but harmony turned out to be a different thing altogether. Every time the sopranos went up and her line went somewhere else, her voice wanted to follow them like a dog slipping its leash.

"Again from the top," said Ms. Tehrani from the front of the sanctuary, where the tall windows made quiet pools of evening light on the stone floor. "Altos, invest all your attention in your own line this time. Don't spend any of it on the sopranos."

Willow gripped her folder tighter. The organ gave them the starting note, and they began. For eight bars it held together, her low part weaving under the high one. Then the sopranos leapt to a long held note, and Willow's ear drifted after it, and suddenly she was singing their melody instead of her own. Worse, she had lost count of where they were in the music. The bar lines might as well have been invisible walls. She stopped, mouth open, staring at the page.

Then she noticed something she had been ignoring all evening. Every time the choir began a new bar, Ms. Tehrani's hand flicked downward, a small, certain motion, and then rose again. Down, up, up, up. Down, up, up, up. She watched for a moment, counting, and it fit. The low point of the hand lined up exactly with the first beat of every bar.

"That's the downbeat," Vincenzo whispered from the next row, following her eyes. He was the one alto who never seemed to get lost.

The choir was still singing, and Willow wasn't. She set her eyes on Ms. Tehrani's hand and waited. Down. She counted the beats silently, one, two, three, four, matching them against the notes on her page, and there it was, the exact spot, the second half of the phrase. She opened her mouth and came in on her low F, right on time, and her part slid back under the sopranos like a drawer closing. She held it against them all the way to the end, even when their line curved sweetly upward and pulled at her.

Ms. Tehrani lowered her hands and smiled at the back row. "That's the sound. A resilient harmony, that's what that is. You came back stronger than you went out." On the walk home, Willow hummed both parts at once, just to see if she could, and found that she could.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many U.S. schools require a sports physical, a checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before a student is allowed to try out or practice with a team.
story:
The list on the rink door was short, and Charles counted it three times to make sure. Twelve names for hockey tryouts, and Eva-Rose's name was not one of them, even though she could skate backward faster than most kids could skate forward. That was bizarre. He laced his skates slowly, watching her sit in the stands with her helmet on her lap like a sad, shiny bowl.

"Maybe they made a mistake," said Augustin, thumping down beside Charles on the bench. "Maybe the coach hates excellence."

"The coach high-fived her last week," Charles said. He presumed there was a reason, because there was always a reason, even when nobody told you what it was. He thought about it while he did his stretches. Eva-Rose had been at the doctor's office on Tuesday; he'd seen her in the waiting room through the window when he rode past on his bike. She had waved with a magazine in her hand. And Mr. Kovalenko, who ran the rink, had been carrying a stack of yellow papers that same afternoon, muttering about signatures.

At the first water break, Charles skated over to the boards. "Mr. Kovalenko, what are the yellow papers?"

"Physical forms," Mr. Kovalenko said. "Every school around here makes a kid get a sports physical before they can even step on the ice for tryouts. A checkup, signed by a doctor. No form, no tryouts."

Charles looked up at the stands. Eva-Rose had her skates on, laced tight, and her stick was right there beside her, and she still couldn't play. It wasn't about skating at all. It was about a piece of paper. "So if she got the checkup but the form's sitting at home on the kitchen counter," he said slowly, "she's out?"

"Signed form or nothing," said Mr. Kovalenko. "Rules are rules, young peasant." He said this because Charles's jacket had a big buckle on it that made him look, apparently, like a farmer from an old book, and Mr. Kovalenko never let that joke die.

Charles borrowed the rink phone, called Eva-Rose's mother, and explained the whole thing twice because the zamboni was roaring in the background. Ten minutes later a car screeched into the parking lot and Eva-Rose's mother ran across the ice parking lot in office shoes, waving a yellow paper over her head like a flag of victory.

Eva-Rose was on the ice before her mother reached the door. She took one lap, backward, arms crossed, smug as anything, and stopped in front of Charles in a spray of snow.

"You presumed correctly," she said, and flicked a chunk of ice at his shoulder. "Now try to keep up, peasant number two."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: For most swimmers, most of the forward push in front crawl comes from the arms, while the kick mainly keeps the legs high and the body balanced.
story:
The note appeared on the soccer field on Monday, tucked into the cone bag when Aubrey lugged it out for practice. Swim assessment Friday, it read. Twenty-five metres, front crawl, side breathing. Anyone who cannot complete it joins the winter conditioning group instead of the travel team. Aubrey read it twice, then stuffed it in her sock, because her weakest skill had just been given a deadline.

She could swim. She just could not swim far, and she did not know why. On Tuesday she went to the community pool where Caelan and Darius already had lanes reserved. "Watch me," she said, and set off determined to power across with her legs, churning the water into foam. By halfway she felt like her thighs were full of sand, and she grabbed the lane rope, gasping. Darius leaned over from the next lane. "You kicked your whole tank empty," he said.

Aubrey hung on the rope and thought. Caelan swam past her, barely fluttering his feet, pulling with long easy arm strokes and breathing to the side, and he reached the wall without slowing at all. Maybe the answer was not her legs at all. "Paraphrase what you just did," she called to him. "What are your feet even for?" He pushed off the wall and floated on his back to answer. "For most swimmers the arms do most of the pushing," he said. "The kick mainly keeps your legs high and your body balanced."

So she tried it his way, thinking arms arms arms, letting her legs flutter gently behind her instead of fighting. The first length was clumsy; she swallowed water on a breath and had to stop. The second was better. By Thursday evening she could make twenty metres before her rhythm fell apart, and Darius timed her from the deck, shouting splits. Afterward the three of them sat in the bleachers with juice boxes, and the orange tasted like nectar after all that chlorine. "Tomorrow," Darius said, "you'll be spontaneous off the blocks and shock everyone." "I will absolutely not be spontaneous," Aubrey said. "I have a plan."

Friday came, cloudy and cool, and the team crowded the pool deck. When her heat was called, Aubrey fixed her eyes on the far wall, counted her strokes, and breathed to the right like Caelan had shown her, arms reaching, legs skimming along behind her. The wall arrived under her hand sooner than she expected. She looked up at the clock, then at her friends bouncing on the deck, and shouted, "Twenty-five metres!"

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Frying an egg is a chemical change, because heat permanently changes the proteins in the egg white so it turns solid and white.
story:
Vincent had failed the last science quiz so badly that his mother had arranged a tutor, and now he sat in Mr. Smith's garage every Tuesday afternoon, staring at a poster that said PHYSICAL CHANGE versus CHEMICAL CHANGE. He wanted to get it, he really did, but the words kept sliding around in his head like water on a hot pan. Isa and Kylie came too, because Mr. Smith said they could work together.

"Melting is easy," Kylie said, turning a piece of candle wax over in her fingers. "It goes soft, then it goes hard again when it cools. Nothing is lost."

"But burning is different," Vincent said slowly. "Because after something burns, you can't get it back." He picked up a rusty nail from the tray Mr. Smith had set out. "And rusting. The nail is never just a nail again."

Mr. Smith, who was sanding a table leg and pretending not to listen, smiled at the wall socket. "Show me you know the difference," he said. "Cook something."

So they did. Isa brought a hot plate from her kitchen, Kylie brought two eggs, and Vincent cracked one onto the pan while the other kids crowded close. The clear, wobbly egg white spread out, then went opaque and white, then solid. Vincent slid it onto a saucer and waited, chin on his fists, while it cooled. It stayed white. It stayed solid.

"It won't go clear again," he said. "It cooled all the way down and it's still like this." He looked up, defiant against his own doubt. "The heat permanently changed the proteins in the egg white. So it's a chemical change. Frying an egg is a chemical change."

Isa wrote it down like it was treasure. Mr. Smith set down his sandpaper and clapped twice.

At the next quiz, Vincent stared at question seven, about a candle burning down and a riverbank that might erode, and felt his pencil move without any fear at all.

"Question eight," Kylie whispered behind him in the hall afterward. "The egg?"

"Chemical," said Vincent. "Easy."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted.
story:
Mila bounced on her toes outside the gym doors, clutching her notebook like a shield. The science fair was bigger than she had imagined: three long rows of folding tables, a volcano already dripping foam, and Tobias waving at her from a poster that read, in extravagant silver letters, "PLANTS LIKE MUSIC!"

"You have to come see this," Tobias said. "My mom's fern grew two whole leaves while I played it guitar."

Mila squinted at the poster. There was a photo of the fern, a photo of the guitar, and nothing else. "But how do you know it was the music? Maybe it just grew because it's spring."

Before Tobias could answer, Ms. Mensah stopped at their table. She read the poster, then tapped it with one finger. "Plants like music. Interesting claim. How would you test it?"

Tobias opened his mouth, then closed it. Mila felt her brain spin, and suddenly she was back in her grandmother's kitchen in September, watching her grandmother say, "If I water this half of the garden and leave the other half dry, then the dry half will wilt." She had called it a hypothesis, a guess written so you could check it. "If, then," she had said, tapping the sentence on paper. "What you change, and what you predict."

Mila blinked and she was at the fair again, the gym humming around her. "A hypothesis," she said. "If you play music for one plant and keep another one quiet, then the music plant will grow more. You change one thing, and you predict the result. Then you watch what happens, and the plants can prove you wrong."

"Two identical plants," Tobias said slowly, his eyes going wide. "Same pot, same window, same water. One gets guitar, one gets silence." He grabbed a marker and started writing across the silver letters.

Ms. Mensah smiled and moved on to the volcano, where Jayce was frantically mopping foam off the table. "Your critique, when you're ready, is that the baking soda ratio needs work," she called over the hissing.

Mila was already flipping to a blank page in her notebook. "Start writing," she told Tobias. "If, then."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
Louis stood at the edge of Ms. Fortin's crowded living room holding a bowl of his mother's potato salad, searching for the new Japanese exchange student, Haruki. Actually, it was Haruki's grandparents Louis wanted to find, because three nights ago Louis had bowled to them at the school welcome and he couldn't stop replaying it. He had bent forward maybe an inch, the way he bowed to the principal in the hallway playfully, and the grandfather had returned a slow, deep bow that seemed to go on forever. Louis had straightened up too fast and stuck out his hand. Nobody had said anything was wrong. But something about the difference bothered him like a word stuck on the tip of his tongue.

"There they are," whispered Nya, nodding toward the kitchen doorway. "Remember in science when Ms. Fortin said a single neuron can't do much, but a whole network figures things out? You need more data, Louis. Watch them greet other people first." Emma, who badly wanted to impress Haruki's grandmother because the woman was a real painter, was already clutching her sketchbook like a shield. "I'll come with you," Emma said, "but you're doing the talking. Last time you almost knocked over the samosas."

So Louis watched. He watched Haruki's grandfather greet Ms. Fortin with a quick, shallow dip of the head, and greet an elderly neighbour with a long, deep bow that the neighbour matched exactly. A pattern began to form in Louis's mind, quiet but certain: bowing was a greeting, and the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it showed. His own inch-bow had been the shallow, quick kind. To the grandfather. He tested the idea when the grandmother approached the food table; he took the potato salad in both hands, and instead of a handshake, he bowed slowly and held it, until his view of the carpet blurred. When he came up, the grandmother was smiling, and the grandfather gave a small nod as if a question had finally been answered.

"You learned," the grandmother said, offering Louis a mochi from her own plate.

Emma slid her sketchbook across the table toward her. "Could you sign page one?"

"Only if the boy bows like that again," the grandmother said, eyes twinkling.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from shale, and it splits into thin flat sheets, which is why it has been used for roofs and chalkboards.
story:
The science room smelled like vinegar from somebody's forgotten volcano project, and Emma stared at the three rocks Mr. Mansour had set on her tray. One was speckled and glassy, one was made of stripes like a sandwich, and one was gray and split into thin flat sheets, like a stack of frozen pancakes pressed together. The class had to sort them into igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic, and Mr. Mansour refused to give any hints.

"Remember," he said, walking between the desks, "you can't watch a rock form. You have to reason backward from what you can see."

Mackenzie leaned over from the next table. "The flat gray one is obviously sedimentary. It's in layers."

Emma turned the gray rock over in her hand. The layers bothered her, though. Sedimentary layers felt like separate pages, but this rock split into sheets, thin and even, and she remembered why that seemed familiar. Last summer, at her grandmother's house, she had found an old chalkboard in the attic. When she asked about it, her grandmother had said, "That's slate, dear. A metamorphic rock, formed from shale. It splits into thin flat sheets. That's why they used it for roofs and chalkboards."

Emma had thought that was the strangest thing she'd ever heard, a rock on a roof, a rock you could write on. Now she pressed her thumbnail against the edge of the gray rock, and a sheet flaked off, flat and smooth as a dinner plate. She imagined the cafeteria's international cuisine week posters hanging on old slate boards like that, and she imagined rain sliding off slate shingles on her grandmother's steep roof.

"It's metamorphic," she told Mackenzie. "It splits into sheets. I think it's slate, like an old chalkboard."

"That's wild," Mackenzie said. "I thought metamorphic meant the striped one."

"The striped one might be metamorphic too," Emma said, picking it up, "or it could be igneous. I was wrong about the volcano poster being about endangered lizards last week, so I'm checking everything twice now."

Mr. Mansour paused at their table, picked up the little flake Emma had split off, and turned it in the light. He set it back down without a word, but he was smiling as he moved on, and Emma wrote "metamorphic" in her neatest letters beside the gray rock.

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: At the Battle of Adrianople in 378 CE, Gothic warriors defeated a Roman army and killed the eastern emperor Valens.
story:
Cole pressed his finger against the glass case, tracing the wide red band that marked Rome's borders at their biggest. "It goes from Britain all the way down to Egypt," he said. "How does something this huge just break?"

Ms. Chaudhry had given each of them a worksheet with one question on it: use the map to explain why the empire split and then fell. Hawa was already writing fast, and Anders was copying her angle of head, pretending he wasn't. Cole had nothing. Last month he'd done the same thing on a group project, copied Hawa's answer instead of cooperating on the work, and she'd stopped talking to him for a week. He still wasn't sure she'd forgiven him, or that he deserved it.

He looked again. The map had two dates. In one year the empire was one red shape. In the next, a line cut straight through the middle, east and west. The western half looked thinner, its borders dented inward like a dented lunchbox. The eastern half held its shape longer.

"Two halves," Cole said slowly. "One line. Why there?"

Hawa leaned over, wary. "Because they split it on purpose, I think. Two emperors, two halves."

"Okay, but why did the west cave in first?" Cole turned to the war memorial plaque beside the map, a list of battles Rome had lost. He ran his finger down it, testing a simple idea: if an army's defeats were near a border, that border was the weak one. He counted. One battle stopped him cold. At the Battle of Adrianople in 378 CE, Gothic warriors defeated a Roman army and killed the eastern emperor Valens. He read it twice. An emperor. Killed in a battle.

"Wait," he said. "The east lost an actual emperor, and the east still lasted longer?"

"Then my theory's wrong," Cole said, half delighted, half annoyed. "Getting your emperor killed should be the worst thing." He thought about it. Maybe losing one battle wasn't the same as being worn down everywhere. Maybe the west wasn't beaten in one blow, just slowly squeezed until it was impoverished, too broke to pay armies along every mile of that enormous border. An empire wasn't an equation where the biggest loss decided everything.

Anders shrugged. "So what do you write?"

Cole borrowed Hawa's pen without asking, then paused, held it out to her first. She took it, wrote her own note, and handed it back. On his worksheet he wrote: the empire was too big to defend, so it split in two; the west fell slowly, the east survived even its worst day. Then he tapped the plaque. "Valens," he said. "Worst day of his life, and it wasn't even the end."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers, and the animals that eat them are called secondary consumers.
story:
Amelia spread her poster board across the picnic table and drew a fat yellow sun in the corner. Her assignment was due Monday: a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, plus an explanation of what happened if one link vanished. So far she had sun, clover, rabbit, and a red-tailed hawk that sometimes circled above the fence. The last arrow, from rabbit to hawk, wobbled because her hand would not hold still.

"That's not right," said Felicia, squinting at it. "At my uncle's farm I had to sort the animals. The goats and the grasshoppers only ate plants. The fox ate the goats' hay neighbors."

"They're called primary consumers," Zoe said, tapping the rabbit on the poster. "The ones that only eat producers. And the animals that eat them are secondary consumers. So your hawk is a secondary consumer. Or higher."

Amelia wrote the words in careful letters beside each animal. Then she stopped, because something was wrong in the actual backyard, not just on paper. A strip of clover along the fence had gone from knee-high to stubble in three days, and no rabbit could eat that much that fast. She had watched from the window for a whole afternoon and seen nothing.

"Maybe you have to magnify the evidence," Zoe said, and ran home for her magnifying glass. Through it, the bitten stems showed clean, angled cuts, dozens of them, all the same height. Too neat for rabbits. Amelia had an idea, and a way to test it. She strung yarn in a low square around one patch of clover and left another patch open, like a tiny fenced field next to an unfenced one. If something walked in, the fence would stop it. If something smaller lived inside, the fence would change nothing at all.

The next morning the fenced patch was eaten down exactly like the open one. Amelia knelt, heart thumping, and lifted the edge of the old tarp folded beside the shed, where dead leaves had piled up like insulation through the winter. Two round eyes blinked at her from a burrow, and behind them, more eyes. Rabbits. A whole nest of young ones, hidden the entire time, making the rabbits on her poster look like a much bigger problem than she had drawn.

"So if the hawk left," Felicia said slowly, "the rabbits wouldn't be eaten, and there'd be more of them."

"And more of them means the clover disappears faster," Amelia said. She had been sure the mystery was something big. Now she changed her own mind out loud: "I thought a deer was jumping the fence at night. It was the smallest link all along."

She pulled out her colored pencils and drew a dotted circle around the nest in the corner of the poster, with an arrow straight up to the rabbit.

"That's the secret part of the chain," she said, and added one word in capital letters: HIDDEN.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Beans and peas host bacteria in small lumps on their roots, called nodules, that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use.
story:
Landon crouched at the edge of the vegetable plot behind his grandfather's barn, pressing bean seeds into the dirt with his thumb. Douglas had bet him five dollars that nothing would grow in the tired old soil, which had sat empty for years and looked gray as ash. Landon intended to win that bet.

"Rows are crooked," Douglas said, leaning on the fence.

"Beans don't care." Landon patted the last seed down. "And watch, my peas over there are going to do something weird to this dirt."

He had heard his grandfather grumble once that the old garden "always came back strong wherever the peas had been," and that clue had been itching in Landon's head ever since. Something about peas and beans left the ground better than they found it. He couldn't see how, so he planned a test: he would plant beans in the gray dirt, and beans in a pot of store-bought soil, and compare.

Three weeks later Lilyanna rode her bike up the lane just as Landon was on his knees with a trowel. He had dug up one small bean plant from each spot, roots and all, and laid them side by side on a translucent plastic sheet so the sun lit them from below. The pot plant had plain white roots. The garden plant's roots were studded with tiny lumps, dozens of them, like beads on a string.

"Gross," Lilyanna said, delighted. "What are those?"

"Nodules," Landon said. "That's what the bumps are called."

He pointed at the pot plant's smooth roots, then back at the garden ones. Only the plant in the field dirt had the lumps, and that patch was where the old peas used to grow. So the bumps had to be the hidden difference, the thing doing the improving. Inside those little lumps, he told Lilyanna, reading from the crumpled seed packet note he'd copied off the library computer, bacteria were pulling nitrogen out of the air and turning it into a form plants could actually use. Free plant food, made out of thin air.

"So the peas and beans are basically running a factory underground," Lilyanna said.

"A factory that also feeds the worms and the decomposer crew cleaning up down there." Landon replanted the bean carefully, pressing the soil back around it like tucking in a blanket. Then he stood, dusted his hands, and pointed at the far corner of the plot. "Next spring, that whole side gets beans. Every single foot of it."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Maeva sat cross-legged in front of the family computer, the fan humming under the desk and the smell of burnt toast drifting in from the kitchen. She had posted the newest stanza of her creek poem the night before, just four lines about the water turning green in September, and now she wanted to see whether anyone had commented. Her account was private. She had checked the setting twice, the way you check a locked door.

The first surprise was waiting in her messages. Mr. Goldberg, the neighbor whose yard backed onto the creek, had sent her a photo of her own words, screenshotted and cropped. "Nice stanza," he had written. "Reminds me of the creek in 1998." Maeva's stomach dropped. He did not follow her. She had never accepted him. She counted her followers on her fingers: Malcom, Summer, her cousin, and a girl named in her mind only as "the one from art camp," someone she had accepted months ago and barely knew.

She tried to diagnose the problem like her science teacher would, hunting for a hidden cause. Four followers. One post. A screenshot that had traveled somewhere it should not have gone. It had to be one of the four. But which one? She decided to run a test. She wrote a new post, fake but believable: "Lost my lucky elastic band at the creek today. If anyone finds it, it's blue and stretchy." Only a follower could see it. If it came back to her from outside, she would know someone had passed it along.

The answer arrived before dinner. Malcom knocked on the door, holding out his phone with a grin. "Summer says you lost a blue elastic band, and honestly, there are a thousand elastic bands at the creek." Maeva crossed her arms. "How does Summer know? She's the only one I asked directly." Malcom's grin faded. "Okay, so. The art camp girl. She sent it to a group chat I'm in, and I forwarded it to Summer because I thought it was funny." He shrugged. "Your account's private, but she follows you."

"Private is supposed to mean private," Maeva said, her voice tighter than she meant it to be.

"That's what I thought too," Malcom said. "But private just limits who can see your posts. Anyone you already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see. She screenshotted it. That's how it works."

Maeva stared at the floor between them, then at her poem still glowing on the screen behind her. She scrolled to her follower list and found the art camp girl, her thumb hovering over the button.

"Wait," said Malcom. "Before you do that. Can I read the rest of the poem? The creek part. I want to hear it out loud."

She turned the monitor toward him.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
story:
Hudson's guitar lesson had moved into Mr. Bui's garage after school because Mr. Bui's baby slept in the living room. Hudson sat on an overturned milk crate with the guitar on his knee, and Rayne sat on the workbench, watching.

"Play the open string," Mr. Bui said, "then play the twelfth fret. Tell me what you hear."

Hudson plucked the low E string, then pressed the string down just behind the twelfth fret, where two dots marked the wood, and plucked again. He frowned. "That's the same note. But higher."

"It's called an octave," Rayne said, hopping off the workbench. "Fatimah taught me that word on the piano."

Hudson played both notes again. He put his finger at the twelfth fret, looked at the string, then slid his finger down toward the nut. "The twelfth fret is halfway up the string. I can see that." He plucked at the twelfth fret again, then the open string again, then the twelfth fret. Same note, one higher. He borrowed a tape measure from the pegboard, measured the whole string, then measured from the nut to the twelfth fret. Half. Exactly half.

"So when I press there," he said slowly, "only half the string is vibrating. And half makes the octave."

He wanted proof. He slid his finger to the ninth fret, measured, and found it was not half; the note was higher than the open string but not the octave. Only the halfway point gave him that. He tried it on the A string next, pressing at its twelfth fret, and the open A answered back an octave lower.

At the door, Fatimah appeared with her helmet under her arm. "The garage is open, so I came in. What did I miss?"

"Put your ear here," Hudson said, and played the open string and the twelfth fret, one after the other, and waited.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
Emma sat in the waiting room of Dr. Okafor's office, gripping a pamphlet about stress like it might escape. Her stomach had been doing flip-flops since Monday, when the school nurse said the cramps probably had nothing to do with food and everything to do with the word she kept seeing on posters in the hallway: anxiety. That was why Angel had come along, holding two juice boxes and a granola bar as if a snack could fix a nervous system.

"You look like a peasant who lost her whole harvest," Angel said, handing her a juice box.

"Thanks."

"Mr. Chanthavong told us about this," Angel went on. "Remember? Coping means the ways a person handles stress or hard feelings. After a bad day, I run laps around the track. Vigorous ones. Then I sleep like a rock."

Emma turned this over. She'd been testing something without knowing it. On Tuesday, when her stomach hurt worst, she had stayed up until midnight replaying every awkward thing she'd said since fifth grade. On Wednesday she'd made herself go to bed at nine, and the cramps had faded by lunch. Pattern: bad sleep, bad stomach. It wasn't proof, but it was a start. Talking, though, she hadn't tried. Talking felt like setting down something heavy, and she wasn't sure she wanted witnesses.

"Emma Weaver?" the nurse called.

Emma stood up, then turned to Angel. "When this is over, can I tell you the whole thing? The midnight worrying and everything?"

"That's the plan," Angel said. "I'll even share the granola bar."

They walked down the hallway together, and Angel peeled the wrapper before they even reached the door. "Fifty-fifty," she said. "Doctors love statistics."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In German, every noun begins with a capital letter, so "I have a dog and a cat" is written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze."
story:
Tristan sat at Meliane's kitchen table with his German homework spread in front of him. The class had been unanimous about choosing German as their language project, and Ms. Martínez had asked everyone to comply with one rule: describe your family and pets in five full sentences. Tristan had written his five sentences, and now red squiggles ran under almost every line on Meliane's laptop.

"Your German is that bad?" Meliane asked, leaning over his shoulder.

"I don't think so." Tristan pointed at the screen. "Look, it flags 'Hund' and 'Katze' but not 'habe'. And it flagged 'Familie' and 'Bruder' too." He scrolled back to the example Ms. Martínez had pasted at the top of the assignment. Even her sentence had red marks under 'Mutter' and 'Vater'. That was the clue. If his sentences were wrong, hers would be right. If hers were also flagged, the spell-checker wasn't catching mistakes at all, or it was catching something else.

Tristan typed a test sentence: "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze." Red squiggles appeared under Hund and Katze. He changed the first letters to capitals, Hund and Katze, and the squiggles vanished. He tried it again with Schwester, then with Vater. Same thing. "Meliane, I think I've got it. In German, every noun begins with a capital letter." He went through his homework and capitalized each noun. The screen went clean.

Then he looked at Ms. Martínez's example again and laughed. Her nouns were all lowercase. The sample sentence every student had copied from was the one full of squiggles.

"You're going to tell her?" Meliane asked.

"I'm going to fix it." Tristan raised his hand as if the teacher could see him, then emailed her a screenshot of her corrected example. "Best student in the class now. Maybe the mentor."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: Singing in unison means everyone sings the same notes; singing in harmony means different parts sing different notes at the same time.
story:
On Tuesday, Mr. Goldberg split the choir into two groups, and Nevaeh's half started drifting toward the other half's notes like iron filings toward a magnet. "Sopranos, stay on your line," he called from the piano, but Nevaeh could feel her voice sliding anyway. When the second part dropped out and everyone sang the same notes together, the sound went suddenly thin and flat, like a blanket with the stuffing shaken out. That puzzled her. More people singing should mean more sound, shouldn't it? She began to speculate: maybe the problem wasn't how many voices there were, but whether they matched.

At lunch she worked it out with Theresa on a napkin, drawing two wobbly lines that ran together, then apart. "Unison is when everyone sings the same notes," Theresa said, chewing her sandwich. "Harmony means different parts sing different notes at the same time." Nevaeh stared at the napkin. So when her part wandered over to match the altos, the harmony collapsed into unison, and the choir shrank to half its size even though every mouth was still moving. That was the hidden cause. She just needed a way to hold her line against the pull.

She remembered the fall talent show, when Miles had stood beside her backstage with his inhaler, wheezing through what everyone assumed was nerves. It had turned out to be a cat allergy, because the auditorium stored the drama club's props beside the school cat's bed, of all things. Miles had solved it by testing one thing at a time, skipping the props room, then the hallway, until he found the culprit. Nevaeh decided she would test one thing at a time too.

That evening she found a folded note tucked in her choir folder, which was strange, since her folder lived in an eccentric old cabinet with a wobbly door that Mr. Goldberg had named Bruno.
