The note read: "You keep sliding to our notes. Try humming YOUR first note in your head between every phrase, like a fence post you can feel in the dark. From the alto section." No signature. Nevaeh read it three times, folded it back along its creases, and put it in her pocket.

The next morning she tried the fence post trick. Hum, breathe, sing. When the altos came in underneath her, the pull came again, but she pressed her mind against her remembered note and stayed put, and the sound around her opened up, wide and strange and full. Afterward she scanned the alto section, and Theresa slid her own choir folder sideways, revealing a matching napkin tucked inside with two wobbly lines drawn apart.

"You wrote it?" Nevaeh asked, and Theresa just grinned and tapped her own throat. "Fence post," she whispered.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: Ticking the checkbox beside a Scratch variable shows a monitor on the stage, so players can watch the score change.
story:
Charlie had promised Pierre that her game would be ready for the library coding club on Saturday, and Saturday was two days away. The game showed a migratory bird flying south, and the player pressed the space bar to steer it past storm clouds. Every time the bird dodged a cloud, the score was supposed to go up by one. Pierre had tested it on Thursday and said the bird worked, but he had frowned at the screen and asked, "How do I know if I'm winning?"

On Saturday morning Charlie carried the laptop to the back corner of the library, where the club met near the tall windows. Ms. MacLeod was stamping returns at the desk, and the smell of old paper and floor wax hung over the carpet. Charlie set up between Pierre and Jillian and opened her project. She had a block that said "change score by 1" inside an if-then block, and the if-then block checked whether the bird was touching a cloud. She knew the logic was there. She just could not see any of it happening.

"Play it," she told Pierre. He pressed the space bar, steered the bird around three clouds, and then let a storm swallow it. "Nothing," he said. "It's fun, but I can't tell if dodging even does anything."

Charlie wanted to justify her code, to prove it was right, but Pierre's frown said arguing would not help. Ms. MacLeod had told the club that the curriculum for this unit was loops and variables, and Charlie remembered the word "variable" from Tuesday. In the orange block menu she found her "score" variable, listed with a small empty checkbox beside it. On a guess, she clicked the checkbox.

A small box appeared at the top left of the stage. It read "score 0". "Try now," Charlie said. Pierre flew the bird past a cloud, and the box ticked up to "score 1", then "score 2", then "score 3" as he threaded between two more clouds. Jillian leaned over from the next seat. "Wait, what did you click?"

"The little box next to the variable," Charlie said. "Tick it and you can watch the score change."

Jillian copied it onto her own screen and grinned when her number climbed. Pierre flew the whole route without touching a single cloud and ended at "score 17". He slid the laptop back toward Charlie. "Now make the bird go faster every ten points," he said.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Iron rusts when it reacts with oxygen in the presence of water, forming a new substance called iron oxide.
story:
Jeremy found the trowel half buried in the flowerbed behind Grandpa's house, and the blade was orange and rough, like it had grown a crust. In the shed, hanging on a nail, sat another trowel that looked almost new. He carried both to the porch steps and set them side by side.

"Grandpa, why is this one rusty and that one isn't?" he asked.

Grandpa came out wiping his hands on a rag. "The rusty one sat out in the garden all winter. The other one stays in the shed, nice and dry. I keep meaning to retire the old thing, but it still digs." He went back inside, and Jeremy stayed on the steps, turning the two tools over. He had a science test coming, and Ms. Chukwu had drawn two columns on the board: physical change and chemical change. Melting ice was physical, she had said, because the water was still water. Rusting was different. He wanted to see the difference for himself.

He got three jar lids from the kitchen, with Grandpa's permission, and a sponge. In the first lid he put the old trowel, dry. In the second he put a piece of steel wool, dry. In the third he put steel wool soaked with water from the garden hose. He lined them up on the porch rail and checked them every day after breakfast. On Thursday, the wet steel wool had gone brown and flaky, and when he pinched it, orange dust came off on his fingers. The dry wool looked the same. The dry trowel looked the same.

Eliam biked over on Saturday, and Jeremy showed him the three lids. "See, water has to be there," Jeremy said. "The iron reacts with oxygen in the water's presence. The dry stuff didn't change at all." He scraped the flaky powder into a small envelope and wrote on it in pencil.

"What's the powder called?" Eliam asked.

"Iron oxide," Jeremy said. "It's a new substance. That's why rusting isn't like melting. When ice melts you still have water. When iron rusts, you don't have iron anymore, not really." He held the envelope up to the sun and the orange dust glowed inside the paper like a tiny sunset.

"Take it to Ms. Chukwu," Eliam said.

Jeremy put the envelope in his back pocket, careful not to crease it, and ran inside to find his shoes.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Canada, a federal bill must pass three readings in both the House of Commons and the Senate before it can receive royal assent.
story:
Piper had one job while her mom stood in the line at the school gym turned polling station: finish her civics sheet before the line reached the voters' table. She sat on the bleachers with her phone, refreshing the parliament website for the fourth time.

"Still on second reading," she reported to Yasmin, who was sitting beside her with a bag of cheese popcorn. "Senate side. So it already did three readings in the House of Commons, then it came over here, and it's done one, two of three. Then royal assent."

"That is a significant amount of reading for one bill," Yasmin said solemnly. "Does it get homework too?"

"Very funny." Piper drew a grid on her sheet: House across the top, Senate below, three boxes each, plus a little crown at the end for royal assent. Seven boxes. She was tracking a real bill, a proposed law about protecting bee habitats, and every time a box got checked off, something real changed in the world. She found that thrilling in a way she could not fully explain.

Flashback to September: she had tried to replicate her social studies teacher's diagram of how a bill becomes law, from memory, on a quiz, and had drawn a straight line from "bill" to "law" with one arrow labeled "stuff happens." Ms. Murphy had written "see me" in red pen. Piper had expected a lecture. Instead Ms. Murphy had pulled up the actual website and said, "Track a real one. It'll teach you better than I can." Piper had walked out of that classroom feeling like she'd been handed a secret map.

Now Anayah appeared from the voting line, sent over by Piper's mom. "Your mom says you have to explain this to me so I stop asking her."

"Okay, so." Piper pointed at her grid. "The bill has to pass three readings in both the House of Commons and the Senate. Six readings total before it even gets to royal assent, which is when it officially becomes law."

"Like a jury has to agree?" Anayah asked. "Twelve people, all saying yes?"

"Sort of, but two whole chambers saying yes, three times each."

Piper refreshed the page one more time, and her stomach dropped. The status had changed, but not the way she wanted. Second reading in the Senate had failed, weeks of progress vanished, the bill dead. She stared at the screen.

"It can just die?" Yasmin leaned over. "After all that?"

"That's the twist nobody tells you," Piper said. "Seven boxes, and any one of them can be the end."

Her mom waved from the line. "Piper! I'm next!"

Piper stuffed the phone in her pocket, popcorn crumbs and all, and whispered, "New bill. Monday. I'm tracking a new one."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator; some small animals survive winter in tunnels under the snow.
story:
Michael had planned to prioritize his science project that morning, but the radio said school was closed, and by ten o'clock he was pulling his sled toward Hollow Park, where Franklin and Violet were already packing snow into walls.

"Fort needs a roof," Franklin said, stomping a block into place.

They dug into a drift beside the playground instead, hollowing out a cave just big enough for the three of them. Inside, out of the wind, Michael pulled off one glove and held his bare hand near the wall. It wasn't warm, exactly, but it wasn't the stinging cold from the open field either. He thought about that. Snow was frozen, so it should feel like ice. He pressed his mitten into the wall and watched it spring back, full of tiny gaps.

"It's mostly air," he said slowly. "Fresh snow, I mean. Look, it squishes. It's like a blanket made of trapped air." He remembered something from a library book about winter, and the pieces fit together. "That's why it feels less cold in here. All that air keeps the heat in."

"So we're basically inside a blanket," Violet said, yawning. "That's why I feel lethargic. My brother says there's a hormone that makes you sleepy when it gets dark this early."

They sat in their dim white room, listening to the wind scrape over the top while their cave stayed still and quiet. Then Franklin poked a stick through the back wall to make a window, and the stick dropped into empty space.

"There's a hole back here," he said.

Michael leaned over and shined his phone light through. Beyond the wall ran a thin tunnel, about as wide as his thumb, curving down into the drift. Then another crossed it, and another, a whole lacy network of passages under the snow.

"Small animals do this," Michael whispered. "The book said some of them survive the whole winter down there, in tunnels under the snow. I thought it meant deep underground."

"We're on top of somebody's house," Violet said.

They all went very still. Somewhere below them, faint as a heartbeat, something small was moving.

"Everybody out," Franklin said. "Slowly."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
story:
Joshua pushed his peas around his plate and waited for the right moment. His dad had come home from the gas station grumbling, and Joshua had been saving his question all through dinner.

"The pump said three dollars and eighty-nine cents today," his dad said to his mom. "Last week it was forty cents less. I nearly swallowed my gum."

Joshua set down his fork. "Dad, what makes the price change? The gas is the same gas, right?"

His dad shrugged. "Ask me why the wind blows. It just does."

But Joshua couldn't let it go. At school the next day, he cornered Ilya and Hussain by the lockers. Ilya's family ran a convenience store, so if anyone knew prices, it was her.

"My dad says gas jumped again," Joshua said.

Ilya pulled out her phone. "My dad checks this stuff. Look." She showed them a chart with a wiggly line going up and up. "That's the price of crude oil. It's what gasoline gets made from. My dad says in the United States, crude oil is usually the biggest single part of what you pay for a gallon of gas."

Hussain frowned at the screen. "So when the wiggly line climbs..."

"The pump price climbs with it," Ilya said. "That's why my dad inhales his dinner whenever he sees the news. He worries the delivery costs will climb too, and then people get grumpy at him about candy bar prices, like it's his fault."

Joshua stared at the chart. It was like finding the hidden spring inside a clock. You couldn't see the cause at the pump, but it was there, underneath, doing the pushing. He wanted to test it.

That weekend, he watched his dad's truck like a hawk. When Ilya's chart dipped for a few days in a row, Joshua counted quietly and waited. On the eighth day, his dad came home whistling.

"Guess who filled the tank for cheap," his dad announced at dinner. "Down twenty cents. Maybe I'll take you boys to the lake Saturday."

"Can Ilya and Hussain come?" Joshua asked. "Ilya's the one who figured out why the price dropped. It follows the oil price."

His dad raised an eyebrow, then smiled. "Smart kid. Sure, she can come. Load of bikes in the truck, then."

Saturday morning, Joshua lugged Hussain's bike up into the truck bed, careful not to scratch it, because Hussain's hands were full carrying the cooler for everyone. Ilya climbed in last, holding a bag of day-old donuts from her dad's store.

"Gas station's on the way," Joshua's dad called through the window. "Pump price is still holding steady. Now I know who to ask before I fill up."

"Ask the chart," Ilya said, and held up her phone as the truck pulled out of the driveway.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Fractions can only be added directly when their denominators match, because the denominator names the size of the pieces being counted.
story:
Brooke slid her worksheet across the table and stared at the first problem: one half plus one third. She wrote an equals sign and then, because something had to go on the other side, she wrote two fifths. It looked tidy. It looked wrong, too, in a way she couldn't name.

Across the room, sunlight passed through Katarina's water glass and refracted onto the ceiling in a wobbly rainbow. Katarina was watching it instead of her own paper, so Brooke nudged the glass a centimeter. The rainbow jumped. "Do that again," Katarina whispered.

"Not until I figure this out." Brooke tapped her pencil. "I added the top numbers and then the bottom numbers. Two fifths. But when I bake with my grandpa, I never see two fifths of anything."

Maeve leaned over from the next table, chewing the end of her braid. "What do you see when you bake?"

"A half cup and then a third cup, when we run out of the big measuring cup." Brooke stopped. She could picture the measuring cups lined up on the counter, the half one chunky and wide, the third one slimmer. The pieces were different sizes. That was it. Halves and thirds weren't the same kind of piece, so counting them together was like counting apples and shoes. Fractions could only be added directly when their denominators matched, because the denominator named the size of the pieces being counted. "The bottoms aren't the same," she said slowly. "That's why I can't just add them."

Mr. Lindqvist wandered past with his coffee mug, which said WORLD'S ADEQUATE TEACHER. He gave her a venomous look, which was unfair, because she had not actually asked him anything. "Figure it out yourself," he said cheerfully. "You're three quarters of the way there."

"That's a fraction," said Katarina.

"Denominator four," said Maeve. "Nice solid number."

Brooke drew two rectangles on scrap paper. She split the first into two parts and shaded one. She split the second into three parts and shaded one. Then she tried something: she cut the first rectangle into six pieces too, and the second one into six as well. Suddenly she had three little pieces on one side and two little pieces on the other, all the same size. Three sixths plus two sixths. Five sixths. She checked it against the measuring cups in her head, one half cup poured into thirds, and it fit.

"I got five sixths," she announced, a little louder than math club usually allowed.

"Show me," said Maeve, dragging her chair over. Katarina brought her water glass so the rainbow landed on the scrap paper, wiggling over the shaded pieces like a tiny spotlight.

"You have a strong constitution," Mr. Lindqvist told Brooke from the doorway, "surviving unlike denominators on a Tuesday." He held up his mug as if toasting her.

Brooke grinned and pulled the worksheet back. She flipped the paper over and wrote a new problem for herself, one fourth plus one third, and slid it toward Katarina. "Your turn. Cut the rectangles."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Scoring a line on thick card with a blunt tool before folding it gives a straight, clean fold instead of a cracked, bumpy one.
story:
Kaylee spread her supplies across the library table: thick cream card, a ruler, glue, and the half-finished birthday card for her grandmother. The plan had seemed simple. Fold the card, glue on the pressed flowers she had collected last spring, and write a poem inside. But every time she folded the card, the paper cracked along the crease, leaving a ragged white line that looked like a scar.

"You're making that face again," said Harrison, sliding into the chair across from her with his own project, a paper airplane so precise it looked like it came from a factory.

"Look." Kaylee folded a spare piece of the card and ran her thumbnail along it to flatten the crease. When she opened it, the surface had split into bumpy flakes. She had tried folding slowly, folding fast, pressing with the ruler's edge. Cracks every time. She only had four sheets of the card left, and the card had to be finished by Saturday, because her grandmother was moving to the retirement home then and Kaylee wanted it waiting on her nightstand.

Klara arrived with a stack of craft books she had hunted down in the nonfiction section. "I figured the answer had to be in one of these," she said, dropping them on the table. "The librarian showed me where the bookmaking ones migrate to, over by the drawing shelf."

Kaylee flipped through a book about handmade books. On one page, a diagram showed a card being folded, but the step before the fold was strange: someone dragging a dull, rounded tool down a ruler's edge to make a shallow groove in the paper. The caption said that scoring the line with a blunt tool first gives a straight, clean fold instead of a cracked, bumpy one. She read it twice. She had been doing the opposite, pressing hard with her sharp thumbnail after the fold.

"That looks backwards," Harrison said. "You use the dull thing before you fold?"

"Scoring," Kaylee said. "You score the line first."

She had nothing blunt in her bag, so she borrowed a dead ballpoint pen from the front desk, the kind with no ink left at all. She lined up the ruler where the fold belonged, drew the dry pen tip along the edge once, and made a shallow groove in the thick card. Then she folded along it. The card bent smoothly, the crease flat and sharp, not a single crack. She held it up to the light. "It actually worked."

Klara leaned over the three sample cards Kaylee had ruined earlier, comparing them to the clean one. "The cracked ones all split right down the middle, exactly where you folded. Same spot every time."

Kaylee nodded. Her analysis of the failures matched: the cracks were not random, they followed her creases line for line. The card had been too thick to fold cold, but it would follow a groove she gave it. With only four sheets left, she could not afford another mistake, so she practiced the scoring motion on the last cracked sample until the pressure felt even, keeping the speed of the stroke proportional to how firmly she pressed. Then she scored the real card, one smooth pull, folded it, and watched it close like it had a hinge.

She spent the next hour gluing the pressed violets and copying out the poem in her best handwriting. When she was done, she set the card upright against the book stack so Klara and Harrison could see it.

"For Grandma," Kaylee said, and ran her finger down the perfect crease.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Jaxon was lying on the rug in Kalen's bedroom, holding Kalen's phone, trying to get the perfect shot of the two of them with Kalen's new skateboard. Kalen's little brother had broken his arm last summer doing a trick off the porch rail, and the doctor had said something about how the cartilage in a kid's wrist is softer than bone, which was why it bent before it snapped. That was the whole reason Kalen's mom had finally bought him a proper helmet. Kalen wanted photographic proof that he owned it.

"Post it to the skate group," Kalen said, peeling off his helmet and dropping it on the bed. "Everyone's posting their setups today."

Jaxon scrolled through the filters, then paused with his thumb over the share button. Something in the corner of the photo was bothering him. He zoomed in, pinching the screen, and there it was: Kalen's front porch behind them, and right above the door, small but readable, the house number, 4122. Beside the steps, the edge of the street sign showed too, Maple Court.

"Wait," Jaxon said. "Don't most people in that group go to our school?"

"Yeah, like fifty kids. Why?"

Jaxon turned the phone so Kalen could see the zoomed-in corner. "Look. Your house number. And your street sign. If somebody in that group isn't actually a kid from school, they could figure out exactly where you live." He had been hesitant to say it at first, because it sounded like something a worried parent would say, but now that the numbers were filling the screen, it seemed obvious. The photo wasn't just a picture of a skateboard. It was a picture of an address.

Kalen took the phone and stared. He scrolled down the group's member list, all the way to the bottom, and found three accounts with no names and no pictures. He tapped one, but it showed nothing, just a blank page. "Anybody could be in here," Kalen said slowly. "Even people none of us know. And it would stay there, right? Posts don't go away when you close the app."

"They persist," Jaxon said. "My dad said that once. Even if you delete it later, other people might have already copied it or shared it."

Kalen sat down on the bed next to his helmet. He was quiet for a second, then he stood up, grabbed the skateboard, and carried it into the hallway where the wall was plain white with no windows. "Come on," he said. "New photo. Same helmet, same smile, no street sign."

Jaxon framed the shot and grinned. "Say four-one-two-two," he said, and pressed the button.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Streaming video uses far more mobile data than sending text messages, so watching videos away from Wi-Fi can use up a data plan quickly.
story:
Kayla's new phone felt warm in her pocket, like it had its own heartbeat. She had earned it by walking the neighbour's dog every single afternoon since September, and on the Saturday her mother finally took her to the mall to pick a case, she chose a purple one with a cartoon frog on it, even though Sandrine said frogs were for little kids.

"It's not for little kids," Kayla said. "It's a toxic frog. Look at its eyes. That frog has seen things."

They found Samy at the food court, holding his own phone under the table so Ms. Jean-Louis, who taught science at their school and happened to be eating a pretzel two tables away, wouldn't spot it. For the whole next week, Kayla rode the bus to school watching video after video, cat compilations, origami tutorials, a documentary about ants that Samy had recommended. Her technique was to download nothing and just stream everything straight from the internet, which felt like magic.

Then, on Friday morning, the videos stopped. The phone loaded and loaded, and a little message appeared saying her data was gone for the month. All of it, in one week.

"My phone's broken," Samy said when she showed him at lunch. "That happened to my cousin. You have to get a new one."

Kayla frowned at the screen. It wasn't broken, she decided, because the texting still worked perfectly. She sent Sandrine a message with seventeen frog emojis and it flew through in half a second. So the phone worked. Something else had run out, and whatever that something was, the videos had eaten it and the texts had barely touched it. She thought about the little bar graph in the settings app, the one she'd never really looked at, and decided to run a test.

That evening she made her mother recount the plan aloud at the kitchen table: how much data they got each month, and how fast it had disappeared. Then Kayla asked her mother to watch one single video on the bus ride to her grandmother's, without Wi-Fi, and check the graph before and after. The bar dropped noticeably. Then her mother sent thirty text messages and checked again. The bar barely moved. Kayla sat back, feeling something click into place. "So that's it," she said. "Streaming video uses way more mobile data than texts. That's why a week of videos on the bus ate the whole month."

"It's not broken," Samy admitted on Monday, when she explained it to him at the mall while they waited for Sandrine outside the arcade. He changed his mind so completely that he immediately deleted three video apps and declared himself a "text-only philosopher." Ms. Jean-Louis walked past, glanced at Kayla's frog case, and said, "Nice frog."

Kayla held the phone up so the screen faced her. "Next month," she told it, "we download at home on the Wi-Fi, and on the bus, you get exactly one ant documentary." The frog on the case stared back at her with its tired, ancient eyes.
